footer.scope: Robot Tuner is for differential-drive robots: two driven wheels, or four-wheel skid steer with the left and right pairs driven together, with wheel encoders and 1 to 5 distance sensors. Mecanum, omni-wheel, car-like (steering) robots and robots without encoders are out of scope.
footer.offline: Runs in your browser. Works offline once loaded.
home.title: Home
home.h1: Tune your robot until it drives the middle of the corridor.
home.lead: Describe your robot, measure it over USB, and find PID gains in a simulator that uses the same physics as our research. You see what every gain does before you try it on the real robot.
home.in_1: Differential drive: 2 driven wheels (plus a caster), or 4-wheel skid steer with the left pair and the right pair driven together.
home.in_2: Wheel encoders on the driven wheels.
home.in_3: 1 to 5 distance sensors (VL53L0X, VL53L1X, Sharp IR, HC-SR04, or your own values).
home.f_builder: Draw your robot from above: body, wheels and where each sensor looks.
home.f_measure: Plug in USB and let the robot measure its own speed, lag, track width and sensor noise.
home.f_corridor: Set up the corridor: its width, wall errors, start pose and noise.
home.f_train: Let the computer search Kp, Ki, Kd and the speed, then export C code.
home.f_playground: Move the sliders while the robot drives and compare values side by side.
home.f_troubleshoot: Your real robot wobbles, drifts or reacts late? Find the cause and what to change.
home.f_tutorial: What P, I and D each do, with small demos you can play with.
home.f_maze: Once the corridor works: test wall following, flood fill and mapping in realistic mazes.
home.how_1: The physics is the C++ simulator of the Simulation-To-Real-Life project, compiled to WebAssembly: distance sensors with their cone, noise, dropouts and reading age; wheel encoders; the firmware's own wheel-speed PID driving a DC-motor model; wheel slip and per-robot build errors. An automatic test checks that the browser gives exactly the same numbers as the C++ program.
builder.intro: Describe your robot as seen from above. The origin is the midpoint between the two driven wheels (the point the robot turns around): +x points forward, +y to the LEFT, angles are counter-clockwise. Everything you change is drawn at once and saved in this browser.
builder.name: Name
builder.drive_4wd: 4-wheel skid steer (left pair and right pair driven together)
builder.front: Front edge ahead of the axle
builder.origin_note: Measure from the axle (the line through both wheel centres) to the front and to the back of the body.
builder.skid_note: A skid-steer robot turns like a 2-wheel robot with a WIDER track: the wheels scrub sideways. The spin test in Measure gives the effective value.
builder.track_eff_note: What the robot really turns with (from the spin test). Starts equal to the wheel spacing; measure it in step 'Spin test'.
builder.sensors_intro: 1 to 5 distance sensors. For centring between two walls you need at least one sensor looking left (angle > 15°) and one looking right (angle < -15°). Drag a sensor on the drawing to move it; Shift + drag rotates it.
builder.step_tau_note: How long a wheel needs to reach 63 % of a new speed (step test). Used by the simple motor model.
builder.timing_note: Loop period = how often the robot decides (set by the sensor rate). Reading age = how old the distance is when it is used. You do not choose these, you measure them; what you choose is the speed.
builder.motor_model_note: The full model runs the firmware's wheel-speed PID on a fitted DC-motor model. If you did not fit a motor model, use the simple lag (it only needs top speed and response time).
builder.file_p: Your robot is one JSON file. Export it to keep it, share it or edit it later; import it on any computer.
builder.hw_p: robot_hardware.txt is the format of the Simulation-To-Real-Life project (tools/gen_hardware.py reads it). Sensor poses are written explicitly.
builder.confirm_new: Replace the current robot? Export it first if you want to keep it.
builder.canvas_hint: Drag: move view · wheel: zoom · drag a sensor: move it · Shift+drag: rotate it
builder.chk_noside: No sensor looks to the side: the robot cannot see the walls it must stay between.
builder.chk_oneside: Sensors look to one side only: use 'follow one wall' mode in the playground (centring needs both sides).
builder.chk_twoside: Left- and right-looking sensors present: centring with PID is possible.
builder.chk_wheels_out: The wheels stick out far beyond the body: they will touch the walls first.
builder.chk_track_eff: Effective track width differs from the wheel spacing by more than 25 %: re-check the spin test.
builder.chk_sensor_out: Sensor #{n} is outside the body outline. Intended?
builder.chk_wheelbase: Axle distance is smaller than the wheel diameter: the wheels would overlap.
builder.chk_range: A side sensor's maximum range is below 15 cm: in a wide corridor it will not see the wall.
builder.source_hint: Where this value comes from: MEASURED (measurement wizard), TYPED (you), DATASHEET or DEFAULT
sensor.note.VL53L0X: Laser time-of-flight, 25° diagonal field of view (18° horizontal), ~33 ms per reading by default.
sensor.note.VL53L1X_short: Laser time-of-flight, 27° diagonal (19° horizontal), short mode: up to 1.3 m, 20 ms budget, 25 ms period. Our robot's sensor.
sensor.note.VL53L1X_long: Laser time-of-flight, long mode: up to 4 m, but at least 33 ms per reading and more sensitive to ambient light.
sensor.note.GP2Y0A21: Analog infrared triangulation. Narrow beam, new value every ~39 ms, noise grows with distance; reads nonsense below 10 cm.
sensor.note.GP2Y0A41: Analog infrared, short range 4-30 cm, ~17 ms per reading.
sensor.note.HC_SR04: Ultrasonic echo, wide beam (~30°). No echo from walls hit at a shallow angle (> ~40° from head-on). Do not trigger faster than every 60 ms.
sensor.f.max_incidence_deg: Max angle to the wall for an echo (0 = any)
corr.intro: Build the corridor your robot must drive: an endless straight corridor with the errors of a real, hand-built one, or a track you draw. The robot uses your robot description and its current PID gains. These settings are also used by the playground and by training.
corr.track_note: The walls are the centre line moved half the width to each side; corners are rounded with the radius. .track files from the Simulation-To-Real-Life project (freeform format) can be imported.
corr.draw_help: Click to add a point, drag a point to move it, right-click (or Ctrl+click) a point to delete it. With "Closed loop" on, the last point joins the first.
corr.errors_note: Real corridors are not perfect. Switch each kind of error on or off and choose its size. Every corridor number gives a different, repeatable corridor.
corr.start_random: Random start (up to the angle above)
corr.start_adjusted_angle: The robot does not fit at this angle: started at {a}° instead.
corr.start_adjusted_offset: Offset reduced so the robot does not start inside a wall.
corr.start_impossible: The robot does not fit in this corridor at all.
corr.to_playground: Tune the gains in the playground →
err.jitter.hint: Small random unevenness along the walls.
err.tilt.hint: Each wall board (40-80 cm) is rotated by a small random angle.
err.bumps.hint: Short things sticking out of the wall (screws, tape, a misplaced board).
err.gaps.hint: Missing wall pieces: the side sensor suddenly sees far away.
err.steps.hint: One wall jumps in or out: the corridor gets wider or narrower.
noise.global_hint: 0 = perfect robot, 1 = like our real robot, 2 = twice as bad.
noise.mismatch_hint: One wheel slightly bigger / its motor stronger. The encoders cannot see it.
noise.delay_hint: Added to the measured reading age: the robot reacts to older data.
noise.angle_bias: Sensors glued on a few degrees off (random per run)
plot.center_err: Centring error (mm, + = left of the centre)
pg.intro: Change the gains while the robot drives and watch the path, the errors and the wheel commands. Try a preset to see a classic mistake, or run a sweep to compare several values side by side from exactly the same start.
pg.kp_hint: Turns harder the bigger the left-right difference is now.
pg.ki_hint: Slowly removes an error that stays (e.g. one weaker wheel).
pg.kd_hint: Brakes the turn when the error shrinks fast: less overshoot.
pg.speed_hint: You choose the speed. Up to 1 m/s: above your robot's measured top speed ({max} m/s) the simulator gives it a faster motor.
pg.units: Error = left distance − right distance (m). Turn = Kp·error + Ki·∫error + Kd·d(error)/dt, in m/s: right wheel = speed + turn, left wheel = speed − turn.
pg.save_gains: Save these gains to my robot
pg.sweep_p: Ghost robots start at the same pose with the same noise; only the chosen value differs.
preset.good.desc: Your robot with its current gains: the reference.
preset.p_low.desc: Kp far too small: the robot corrects so slowly that it drifts along off-centre and nearly touches the wall.
preset.p_high.desc: Kp far too big: every small error causes a big turn, the robot overshoots and wobbles left-right.
preset.no_d.desc: No derivative: nothing brakes the turn as the error shrinks, so the robot swings through the centre line before settling.
preset.i_windup.desc: A big Ki keeps adding up the error during the start manoeuvre; long after the robot is centred the stored integral still pushes it to the other side.
preset.too_fast.desc: Full speed with old sensor data (150 ms extra delay): by the time it reacts it has already moved on. It reacts late and swings.
preset.saturation.desc: Cruising at top speed: one wheel cannot go any faster, so the turn the PID asks for is cut off. It cannot turn back in time.
preset.mismatch.desc: The right wheel is 8 % faster and Ki = 0: P alone leaves a steady offset from the centre. Add some Ki to remove it.
ts.h1: Troubleshooting: on the real robot it does X
ts.intro: Find what your real robot does, read why, try the suggestions one at a time, and open the simulation that reproduces it.
ts.wobble.why: Each small error causes a turn that is too big, so it overshoots the centre again and again.
ts.wobble.try: Lower Kp (halve it).|Raise Kd a little: it brakes the turn as the error shrinks.|Lower the speed.|Check that one sensor is not reading glitches (noise looks like error to P and especially to D).
ts.drift.sym: It drifts slowly to a wall and corrects too late
ts.drift.why: Kp is too small: the turn it asks for is too weak for the error.
ts.drift.try: Raise Kp (double it) until it starts to wobble, then go back a bit.|Check the sign: a wrong sign makes it steer TOWARD the wall.
ts.overshoot.sym: After a disturbance it swings through the centre before settling
ts.overshoot.why: Nothing brakes the turn while the error shrinks.
ts.overshoot.try: Add Kd (start with Kd ≈ Kp / 5).|Lower Kp slightly.
ts.late.sym: It reacts late, as if it saw the wall too late
ts.late.why: Between two decisions the robot moves speed × loop period, and the data is already old (reading age). At high speed that is a lot.
ts.late.try: Lower the speed.|Measure the loop period and reading age (Measure page) and put them in the robot: the sim then shows the real delay.|Make the loop faster: shorter sensor timing budget, no slow code (Serial prints, delay()) in the loop.
ts.cant_turn.sym: It cannot turn back at full speed
ts.cant_turn.why: One wheel is already at maximum: the turn it needs cannot be added, so it is cut off (saturation).
ts.cant_turn.try: Cruise below the top speed (about 70-80 %) so there is room to turn.|Slow down while turning hard (slowdown).
ts.one_side.sym: It always drives a bit off-centre to one side
ts.one_side.why: A constant error: one motor/wheel stronger than the other, or a sensor angle / bias not as you think.
ts.one_side.try: Check the sensor angles and mounting (both side sensors must look equally far forward).|Measure sensor bias (Measure → sensor test) and subtract it.|Add a small Ki to remove a steady offset.|Check the wheel mismatch with the straight drive test.
ts.swing_after.sym: Long after the start it still swings to the other side
ts.swing_after.why: Integral windup: the I term collected a big error during the start and needs a long time to unwind.
ts.swing_after.try: Lower Ki.|Limit the integral (anti-windup limit).|Reset the integral after a big manoeuvre.
ts.gaps.sym: It jerks at gaps or openings in the wall
ts.gaps.why: A gap makes one side sensor read far away: a huge sudden error.
ts.gaps.try: Clip the error (error limit) so one reading cannot command a violent turn.|Ignore sudden jumps of one sensor for a short time (glitch filter).|Turn on 'Gaps' in the corridor errors and test.
tr.intro: The computer drives your robot through a set of corridors many times and keeps the gains that drive most parallel and centred, without crashing, as fast as possible. First a grid search over Kp, Ki, Kd (and speed), then a genetic algorithm refines the best ones — the same method and reward as our research simulator. Takes about 1-5 minutes.
tr.setup: Robot "{name}" in corridors like yours ({w} mm, starts up to ±{a}°, noise ×{n}) plus a narrower, a wider one and an S-bend.
tr.reporting: Testing the best gains at 0×, 1× and 2× noise…
tr.use: Use these gains for my robot
tr.plot_crash: Crash % of the best, per generation
tr.report_p: The best gains on new corridors and starts, with no noise, the noise you set, and twice that.
ms.intro: Connect the robot with a USB cable and let it measure itself, one step at a time. Each step says what it measures, why it matters and what to do. Results go into your robot description (marked MEASURED). No robot or other firmware? Type the values instead.
ms.nosupport: Your browser cannot talk to USB devices. Use Chrome or Edge on a computer, or type the values by hand (manual mode).
ms.manual_note: Every step also accepts typed values, e.g. from your own measurement program.
ms.nofw_h: No firmware that answers these commands?
ms.nofw_p: Flash this minimal Arduino sketch: it answers the same commands (CAL TICKS, CAL MAXSPEED, CAL FF, CAL STEP, CAL DRIVE, CAL SPIN, CAL TOF, STATUS, LOAD SENSORS). Set your pins and sensor code at the top.
ms.connect_first: Connect the robot first, or use manual mode.
ms.type_note: Typed values are saved at once.
ms.physical.title: Measure the robot with a ruler
ms.physical.what: Body size, wheel diameter and width, wheel spacing, axle position, caster and the position and angle of every sensor.
ms.physical.why: The simulator needs the robot's shape to know when it touches a wall, and the sensor poses to know what each sensor sees.
ms.physical.how: Measure from the axle (the line through both wheel centres) in millimetres. Sensor angles: 0° = straight ahead, + = to the left.
ms.physical.p: Enter these in the robot builder; the drawing updates while you type.
ms.ticks.title: Encoder ticks per wheel turn (CAL TICKS)
ms.ticks.what: How many encoder ticks one full wheel revolution gives.
ms.ticks.why: Every distance and speed the robot measures comes from this number.
ms.ticks.how: Motors are off. Mark each wheel, press Start, turn each wheel by hand exactly one turn forward, then press 'Done'.
ms.ticks.ask: Turn each wheel exactly one revolution forward by hand, then press Done.
ms.maxspeed.title: Top speed (CAL MAXSPEED)
ms.maxspeed.what: The wheel speed at full power.
ms.maxspeed.why: The PID cannot ask for more than this. Cruising close to it leaves no room to steer (saturation).
ms.maxspeed.how: Lift the robot so the wheels turn freely (wheels in the air!), with a full battery. Press Start: both wheels run at full power for one second.
ms.ff.title: Motor feed-forward and deadband (CAL FF)
ms.ff.what: The PWM needed to start moving (deadband) and how much PWM each extra unit of speed needs.
ms.ff.why: The wheel speed controller uses these to reach a new speed quickly without waiting for its integral.
ms.ff.how: Wheels in the air. Press Start: the PWM rises step by step (about a minute).
ms.step.title: Wheel response time (CAL STEP)
ms.step.what: How long a wheel takes to reach a new speed (63 % of the step = time constant).
ms.step.why: This lag is part of every steering decision: the robot cannot turn faster than its wheels can change speed.
ms.step.how: Wheels in the air. Press Start: both wheels jump from 0 to a target speed and the response is recorded.
ms.drive.title: Straight drive (CAL DRIVE)
ms.drive.what: Whether 1 m on the encoders is really 1 m (wheel diameter error, left/right difference).
ms.drive.why: Wrong wheel scale = wrong speeds and distances; a left/right difference makes the robot curve.
ms.drive.how: Put the robot on the floor with 1.5 m free in front. Press Start: it drives 1 m by its encoders. Measure how far it really went.
ms.drive.ask: How far did the robot really drive? (metres, e.g. 0.985)
ms.spin.title: Effective track width (CAL SPIN)
ms.spin.what: The wheel spacing the robot really turns with.
ms.spin.why: Turning depends on it. It is usually a bit larger than the measured wheel spacing (tyre contact, scrub); for 4-wheel skid steer much larger.
ms.spin.how: Floor, free space around. Put a mark on the floor under the robot's nose. Press Start: it spins 5 turns by its encoders. Count the REAL turns (e.g. 4.85).
ms.spin.ask: How many turns did the robot really make? (e.g. 4.85)
ms.spin.untrusted: The spin was not symmetric or the motors hit their limit: the result may be wrong. Lower the spin speed and repeat.
ms.tof.title: Sensor noise and bias (CAL TOF)
ms.tof.what: For each sensor: how much the reading jumps (noise), how far off it is on average (bias), how often it gives no reading.
ms.tof.why: Noise is what the D term amplifies; a bias makes the robot drive off-centre.
ms.tof.how: Put a flat board at a known distance in front of each sensor (e.g. 200 mm), robot not moving. Press Start: each sensor takes 200 readings.
ms.tof.ask: True distance from each sensor to its board (mm)
ms.timing.title: Loop period and reading age (LOAD SENSORS + STATUS)
ms.timing.what: Loop period = how often the robot decides. Reading age (delay) = how old the distance is when the decision is made.
ms.timing.why: You do not choose these, you measure them: the loop period is set by the sensor rate. What you DO choose is the speed: the faster you drive, the further the robot moves between two decisions and the older (in centimetres) its data is.
ms.timing.how: Motors are disabled for this test. Press Start: the robot reports its timing 12 times, then the normal profile is restored.
chk.ticks_range: {v} ticks per turn is implausible. Re-check that both wheels turned exactly once.
chk.ticks_lr: Left ({l}) and right ({r}) differ by more than 2 %: one wheel was turned more, or an encoder misses ticks.
chk.speed_range: Top speed {v} m/s is implausible: wheels in the air? battery charged?
chk.speed_lr: Left {l} and right {r} m/s differ by more than 10 %: a weak motor or gearbox.
chk.tau_range: Response time {v} s is implausible: was the target reachable?
chk.track: Track width {v} mm (wheel spacing {g} mm)? Re-check: count the turns again, and make sure the robot spun in place.
chk.tof_std: Sensor {n}: noise {v} mm is high. Is the target flat and not too far / too shiny?
chk.tof_drop: Sensor {n}: {v} % readings missing. Target out of range or at a bad angle?
chk.loop_slow: Loop period {v} ms is slow: the robot decides only a few times per second. Look for slow code in the loop.
chk.age_old: Reading age {v} ms is more than 3 loop periods: the data is old when used.

mz.intro: Test how robust maze-solving algorithms are on YOUR robot, with the same sensor, encoder and motor models as the corridor. Mazes are built wall by wall with small placement errors that add up, like a real hand-built maze. Left: the real maze. Right: what the robot believes (its own map from its sensors and encoders).
mz.cell_hint: Your robot needs at least {n} mm to turn around in a cell.
mz.braid_hint: 0 = perfect maze (one path). More = loops, which defeat simple wall following.
mz.build_err_hint: Each wall is placed relative to its already-built neighbours, so errors add up across the maze. At the default the maze still looks perfect.
mz.algo_note: Algorithms get only sensor readings and encoders, like on the real robot: their map and position drift. The examples look around at each cell with the front sensor and centre between side walls while driving. Raise the noise to see them start failing.
mz.batch_p: Run the algorithm on many random mazes of these settings.
mz.batch_res: Found the exit in {ok} of {n} mazes
algo.wall_follower.desc: Keep the left hand on the wall: turn left if you can, else straight, else right, else back. No map needed; fails in mazes with loops around the exit.
algo.flood_fill.desc: Assume unknown walls are open, compute the distance of every cell to the exit, always move to the neighbour that is closest; recompute as walls are discovered (micromouse classic).
algo.dfs.desc: Depth-first exploration: go to an unvisited neighbour, otherwise go back the way you came, mapping everything on the way.
algo.custom.desc: Write create(ctx, kit) returning {step(obs) -> {left, right}}. See the comments in the template; kit.CellRobot does the driving and mapping for grid algorithms.
home.demo_time: {s} s, same start and same noise for both
home.route_h: Five steps from a robot to working gains
pg.speed_virtual: Faster than your robot can drive ({max} m/s): simulating a stronger motor with the same response time. The real robot cannot do this without new motors.
corr.closed: Closed loop: the end joins the start, the robot drives laps
pg.offset_hint: 0 = middle. The wanted left − right becomes −offset × (1/sin of the left sensor angle + 1/sin of the right one); it does not depend on the corridor width.
